newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgians take Renault protest to the Internet.
newsitem.headline: Belgians take Renault protest to the Internet.

text.p: From Renault Espace to cyberspace may be quite a leap for some, but for Belgian Hans Deveuster the connection between the embattled French carmaker's popular van and the Internet was easy to make.

He took his protest at Renault's disputed decision to close its Belgian plant to the Net, setting up a Dutch-language Website for surfers to e-mail their displeasure and promising to pass their grievances on to its Paris headquarters.

Since the carmaker announced the closure of the plant in Vilvoorde near Brussels a week ago with a loss of 3,100 jobs, Deveuster has received 936 site visits, mainly from Belgium but also from as far afield as the U.S., India and Japan.

"I was in Vilvoorde, training at the athletics club, when I heard the news," the 23-year-old electronics graduate told Reuters, "the way in which the closure was announced made me say: 'this can't be, this can't be allowed'."
Deveuster, who surfs the Net daily, set up the site to collect protests against the sudden announcement, made without warning or consultation as Belgian law requires.

Renault's cold, stroke-of-a-pen decision to eradicate not only 3,100 jobs at the plant but also at least 1,000 at suppliers and subcontractors in a country where unemployment is already high, angered unions and politicians alike.

Numerous Belgian towns on both sides of the Dutch and French language divide have put orders for Renault cars on hold following a decision by the Interior Ministry to suspend an order for 150 Renault Meganes for the state police.
But ordinary Belgians have also lost interest in the make, Belgium's third best selling before the Vilvoorde decision, if Deveuster's Website is anything to go by.

The tone of many of the named reactions, some with their own Internet addresses, is 'Strike Renault Where It Hurts: In The Wallet'. Some visitors lash out at allegations excessive wage costs were behind the decision, most simply call for a boycott.
"I'm glad I don't drive a Renault and I never will," wrote a visitor to the site. "We can do without Renault," another said.

"Everybody should consider buying a VW or an Opel instead of buying a Renault; if everybody did this then those nationalist French would think again," a third said, echoing accusations that Renault axed Belgian jobs to save employment in France.
"Please, no misplaced nationalism," a university professor wrote, trying to quell outbursts of nationalism.
Deveuster vets all e-mail messages for inappropriate language before placing them on the site, but says that apart from a call to smash up Renault there has been no rudeness.
The site has news from a Belgian newspaper and a local agency on the closure and details on upcoming protests.
Attached software also offers visitors the opportunity to find out how many have visited the site, which country they are from and at what the time of the day their contribution was sent in.

Deveuster says he has already faxed several days' worth of reactions to the main metal workers union and plans to hand them personally to Renault Vilvoorde workers occupying the plant and holding hundreds of finished cars and equipment hostage.
He plans to have invitations for reactions in French and English on the site soon to attract international reactions. "It is a very easy medium to send messages, easier than a letter."

Bart Tack, one of the Dutch-speaking visitors to http://club.innet.be/year1915/ told Reuters he would e-mail Renault chief executive officer Louis Schweitzer in person if he could to protest against "his arrogance".
Deveuster says he has scoured Renault's www.renault.com site but found no Internet address for Schweitzer. A notice on the site says, "Opening Soon".
A rival to Deveuster, Michel Mes, set up his own site (http://www.netwise.be/reNO/) to attract comments, also polling many calls for a boycott.
Under the banner "What Belgium Thinks Of Renault", Mes has an animated figure walking across the screen, dropping his shorts and urinating on the Renault logo.
